Sahasra Ravana

Stories from the Ramayana

Sahasra Ravana

Sita Becomes Mahakali — and Faces the Thousand-Headed Ravana

In everyday English — Adbhuta Ramayana, sargas 17–27

Stories by Eku

1 · The Coronation in Ayodhya · · THE CORONATION IN AYODHYA

This story is made to be told — read it out loud, slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home. The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words — change your voice a little as you speak them. The green box — Pause and think — stop there, ask questions, let the listeners speak.

The war in Lanka was over. Rama had returned to Ayodhya, and his coronation had taken place there. Lamps burned in the city, flowers rained down, and every home was full of joy.

In the royal court sat the sages. They were praising Rama — “You defeated the ten-headed Ravana! No battle like it was ever fought before!”

Rama sat quietly, listening. Beside him sat Sita — in a red saree with a gold border, a small gold tiara, her long braid with jasmine flowers. She was smiling — a smile that hid a secret.

Everyone in the court felt the story was now complete. Ravana was dead, Rama was king, and peace had returned to Ayodhya. But Sita knew — the story was not yet complete.

2 · Sita's Revelation · · SITA'S REVELATION

Then Sita spoke softly — “Sages, you are praising Rama — but the Ravana who was killed was not the real Ravana. He was only the younger brother.”

Silence fell on the court. Rama asked — “Sita, what are you saying?”

Sita said — “The ten-headed Ravana had an elder brother — Sahasra Ravana. He has a thousand heads and two thousand arms. He lives on the island of Pushkara — and he is far more powerful than his younger brother.”

Sita told them — when she was small, living in her father Janaka's house in Mithila, a Brahmin had passed through. He was the one who had told her the tale of this elder Ravana.

“The younger Ravana had received Brahma's boon, and Shiva's blessing too — that is why he had become so powerful,” Sita said. “But the elder brother was stronger than him from birth itself.”

Rama heard — and his mind was made up. “If there is one more Ravana, then he too must be fought. Ayodhya's peace will only be complete when he too is defeated.”

Pause and think — Sita said this in front of the whole court — in the middle of Rama's praise. Was that the right time to speak the truth? And this tale had been told to Sita when she was a child — can something heard in childhood still be of use so many years later?

3 · The Voyage to Pushkara · · THE VOYAGE TO PUSHKARA

Rama gathered his army — the monkey army with Sugriva, the warriors of Ayodhya, and the rakshasas of Lanka with Vibhishana. Hanuman came too, Lakshmana came too — and Sita came too.

Boats and ships set out on the sea. The sails filled, the flags fluttered, and the army sailed toward the island of Pushkara.

Hanuman said — “Lord, this enemy is greater than the ten-headed one — but we are with you.”

Rama said — “Hanuman, being together is itself the greatest strength.”

From afar the island of Pushkara appeared — high mountains, dense forests, and in their midst the city of the elder Ravana.

Sahasra Ravana heard that Rama's army was coming — so he too gathered his army of rakshasas. His commanders came to the field, each with his own weapon.

Pause and think — Rama did not go alone — the whole army went with him, and Sita went too. Are great deeds done alone, or together? And Sita going along — was that only keeping company, or something more?

4 · The Battle of Pushkara · · THE BATTLE OF PUSHKARA

The battle began. The monkey army charged forward — lifting trees and mountains and hurling them at the rakshasas. At first the monkeys had the upper hand.

The rakshasa army began to fall back. It seemed as if victory was near.

Then Sahasra Ravana himself came to the field. He loosed the vayavastra — the divine weapon of wind. A great storm rose — and the army scattered. The warriors of Ayodhya returned to Ayodhya, the monkeys to Kishkindha, the rakshasas to Lanka.

Rama was left alone on the field — but he was not afraid. He raised his bow and stood before Sahasra Ravana.

Pause and think — The army was close to victory — and a single weapon changed everything. Is victory in battle always won by strength? And when everyone has left you, to stand alone — is that defeat, or courage?

5 · Rama Falls · · RAMA FALLS

Rama raised the Brahmastra — the divine weapon given by the sage Agastya. But Sahasra Ravana caught it in his hand — and snapped it like a straw.

Rama was stunned for a moment. In that very moment Sahasra Ravana loosed his arrow — and Rama fell to the earth, unconscious.

Silence fell all around. Hanuman and Lakshmana ran to him — but Rama did not rise.

From afar Sita was watching all this. And then she laughed — a laugh in which there was no fear, no mockery. She laughed because she knew what Rama did not yet know — what power slept within her.

Sita said in her heart — “Now the time has come — the power within me must come out.”

Pause and think — Rama was left alone, and even his greatest weapon had broken. Can a new strength hide inside the moment of defeat? And Sita's laugh — was it a laugh of mockery, or of recognising the power within herself?

6 · Sita Becomes Mahakali · · SITA BECOMES MAHAKALI

Sita gave up her human form. From within her came another form — the form of Mahakali, the form of Bhadrakali.

Her form was dark, with many arms, and divine weapons in her hands — the trident and the sword. She was not frightening, she was radiant — like the sky before a storm, like a wave of the deep sea.

The earth trembled. The gods watched from the sky — and understood that something great was about to happen.

The gods said — “This is that very Shakti, without whom no work is done.”

Mahakali moved toward the battlefield — slowly, but with every step the earth trembled.

Pause and think — Until now Sita had been the form of patience and compassion — now she is the form of power. Can one person hold both forms — gentle too, and radiant too? And is power only for battle, or also for protection?

7 · The Thousand Heads Fall ◆ · · THE THOUSAND HEADS FALL

◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it tells of battle and slaying.

In a single moment Mahakali reached the field. And in that same moment the thousand heads of Sahasra Ravana fell to the earth — and the battle was over.

Then Mahakali danced a cosmic dance — on the battlefield, between sky and earth. The Matrikas came with her too — a company of goddesses, who began to dance beside her.

The earth trembled so much that it began to sink. Then Shiva lay down quietly beneath Mahakali's feet — and the earth grew still.

Peace fell on the field. The rakshasa army too was finished — and for the first time there was silence on the island of Pushkara, but that silence was no longer of fear, it was of peace.

Pause and think — Mahakali ended the battle in a single moment — but then she danced, and the earth trembled. Is calming power as needful as awakening it? And Shiva lying down quietly — was that too a way of calming power?

8 · Brahma Explains · · BRAHMA EXPLAINS

The gods felt — if Mahakali did not grow calm, the earth itself would be destroyed. They came forward and begged her to be calm.

Mahakali looked toward the unconscious Rama — “Until Rama wakes, how can I think of the world's welfare?”

Brahma restored Rama's consciousness. Rama opened his eyes — and seeing the radiant form of Mahakali before him, he was startled.

Brahma said — “Rama, do not fear. This is Sita herself. Whatever you do — the making and the guarding of the world — all of it happens only together with this Shakti. Without Shakti no work is done.”

Rama said — “Now I understand — Sita is not only my wife, she is the Shakti who lives within everyone.”

Brahma reassured Rama — this awesome form is no one else, it is Sita herself. Rama's fear left him — and his heart filled with reverence.

Pause and think — Rama was frightened of Sita standing before him — because he could not recognise her true form. Do we too sometimes fail to see the true form of those closest to us? And what did Brahma teach Rama — that power should not be feared, it should be recognised?

9 · The Thousand Names · · THE THOUSAND NAMES

Brahma reassured Rama — and asked Sita, “Who are you, truly?”

Sita said — “I am that Shakti who lives within everyone — who carries one across the ocean of the world.”

Then Sita gave Rama divine sight — and Rama saw her true form. Rama was filled with joy — and he praised Sita — by her thousand names.

Those names are not printed in this book — the full list is in the Adbhuta Ramayana. Know only this — Rama sang one thousand and eight names of Sita, and in each name there was one of her forms.

Pause and think — Rama was given divine sight — only then could he see Sita's true form. Do we sometimes need new eyes to truly see someone — and are those new eyes given by love?

10 · The Return to Ayodhya · · THE RETURN TO AYODHYA

Hearing Rama's praise, Mahakali grew calm. Rama begged — “Now become Sita again.” And Sita returned to her first, gentle form — the red saree, the jasmine braid, the same soft smile.

Rama and Sita sat in the Pushpaka vimana — and returned to Ayodhya.

In Ayodhya Rama told everyone this tale — that the ten-headed Ravana was the younger brother, and the elder Ravana had been defeated by Sita, who became Mahakali.

Pause and think — Rama told everyone this tale — his defeat too, and Sita's victory too. Is telling of one's own defeat also courage? And Sita returned to her first form — does changing form change the person?

11 · Farewell · · FAREWELL

Then Rama bade farewell to Sugriva and the monkey army — and to Vibhishana and the rakshasa army too. Everyone returned to their own homes — the monkeys to Kishkindha, the rakshasas to Lanka.

It is said — whoever hears this tale receives the blessing of Shakti.

And so — peace returned to Ayodhya. But now everyone knew — peace is guarded not only by Rama's bow, but also by Sita's Shakti.

Pause and think — After the farewell everyone returned to their own homes. Does togetherness end, or does the memory of togetherness remain? And Ayodhya's peace — was it the same as before, or was everything new now?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source — Adbhuta Ramayana

The whole story of this book is from the Adbhuta Ramayana, sargas 17–27 — a Shakta Sanskrit work, traditionally linked with Valmiki. In sarga 17 Sita speaks of the elder Ravana in the court; in sargas 18–19 the army gathers; in sargas 20–21 the battle and the scattering of the army by the vayavastra; in sarga 22 the breaking of the Brahmastra and Rama falling unconscious; in sarga 23 Sita's Mahakali form and the slaying of the thousand heads; in sargas 24–25 Brahma's explanation and the divine sight; in sarga 26 Sita's return, and in sarga 27 the return to Ayodhya and the farewell. For the sarga-by-sarga detail this book has relied on a published sarga summary — no direct quotations from the Sanskrit text have been taken.

This Story Is Not in Valmiki's Ramayana

In Valmiki's Ramayana there is no tale of Sahasra Ravana — there the death of the ten-headed Ravana of Lanka is the last battle, and the story ends with the coronation. In the Adbhuta Ramayana Sita's birth is also told differently — from Mandodari — while in Valmiki, Janaka finds her in a field. In this book the Adbhuta Ramayana's tale is never mixed with Valmiki's tale — it is a separate telling.

Sarala Das's Vilanka Ramayana

In the Vilanka Ramayana of the Odia poet Sarala Das (15th century), Sita also defeats the thousand-headed Ravana — but the tale is different. There the Ravana lives in Vilanka (in Patala), Rama goes alone with Hanuman, and Sita, taking the Panchashara from Katyayini, assumes the Trailokya-Mohini form — then Rama kills him. In the Adbhuta Ramayana Sita herself, as Mahakali, cuts off his heads. The two tales are different from each other — this book's main tale is the Adbhuta Ramayana's; the Vilanka Ramayana is only a second telling.

The Thousand Names — Why the Full List Is Not Printed

Rama praised Sita with 1,008 names — that list is in the Adbhuta Ramayana, but it is not printed in this book. This book only tells that Rama sang her thousand names — to read the full list, see the Adbhuta Ramayana.

The Island of Pushkara — What Kind of Place

The island of Pushkara is a distant island kingdom of the Adbhuta Ramayana — do not confuse it with the Pushkar tirtha of Rajasthan. This is traditional geography, not a proven place — and this book presents it in that form.

About the Reel — A Pointer Only, Never a Source

The idea for this book came from an Instagram reel — whatsisasays.folklore, “The thousand-headed Ravan — Part 1”, 2026-11-19. The reel was only a pointer, never a source. Every part of it was checked against the sarga summaries of the Adbhuta Ramayana. Where the reel shortens the tale, the book follows the sarga — the reel says the army scattered “in one breath”; in sarga 21 it is the vayavastra; the reel says Rama “sailed” there; in sarga 18 he goes with his army; the names of those who went with him are taken from the army's make-up.

Shiva's Quiet Form

In sarga 23 it is said that Mahakali's dance made the earth tremble, and Shiva lay down in the form of a corpse beneath her feet, so the earth grew still. In this book that is told quietly and without any frightening detail — no frightening scene is shown.

The Fruit of This Tale

At the end of sarga 27 of the Adbhuta Ramayana it is said that hearing this tale brings merit and benefit. This book tells that in the same form — whoever hears this tale receives the blessing of Shakti.
